<reason>CON executed a clever reframe—nobody defends bans, so the fight is over "same basic terms"—and backed it with plausible technical specifics (no metabolism/withdrawal period, passage drift, medium as the food). But PRO's reading of the motion is the more natural one: "basic terms" plus "once safety standards are met" already builds in the pre-market gate, and equal legal standing under one hazard-based framework (oysters, canned ham, ground beef differ in controls but not in terms) is what "same basic terms" ordinarily means. PRO answered CON's vacuity trap directly in A4.1 by naming concrete violations (name bans, warning labels, procurement exclusion), and caught CON's shift on labeling: B2.8 called production-method disclosure ordinary practice, B2.4 claimed the label clash as a win, then B4.2 retreated to "the label was never what made the regime different." Decisively, CON's own model regime—legalize, inspect, disclose, shelf—is functionally the motion; negating on the ground that the assays differ is a semantic swap rather than a real policy disagreement. CON's closing claim that cell-line authentication and medium approval went unrebutted has some bite, and PRO's closing was thinner on those, but under PRO's already-established HACCP frame they are facility-specific controls, not "different terms." Competitive, but PRO made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A4.1/A4.5 response to CON's B3.1 vacuity dilemma: naming specific non-ban requirements that would violate the motion, then turning CON's own "farm-raised"/"from concentrate" examples (B2.8) against the claim that a truthful origin qualifier constitutes a different regime, forcing CON's B4.2 retreat on the label.</best_rebuttal>
